schools.summary: Gill reads the whirlwind as notice of the Lord's appearing (Targum: 'whirlwind of distress'), and the speaker as Jehovah the Son, the eternal Word, seen in human form.
Henry orders the scene by heads (who, when, how, to whom, what): the eternal Word who spoke from Sinai now interposes 'then,' when all had spoken and none prevailed.
Clarke fixes the word as searah (not suphah), a tempest to fill Job with awe (Chaldee 'whirlwind of grief'); Wesley hears the harbinger of God's presence, sent to humble Job and his friends alike.
Ellicott calls the chapter the grand climax of the poem, the argument drawn from man's ignorance, the tone throughout mingled with reproach though Job is later justified (42:8).

themes: the speaker is the eternal Word

schools.summary: Gregory finds the reason for the reproof: since Job is to live on and receive double, God must humble him lest his very victory slay him with the sword of pride, the consciousness of virtue being the soul's deadliest peril.
Gill takes the rebuke as aimed at Job, not Elihu, God wondering that such a man should so speak.

Keil reads zeh as intensifying 'who,' the participle showing Job interrupted mid-speech, 'counsel' put for 'my counsel,' the word coming 'out of the storm' (a spelling found only here and 40:6); Ellicott answers 'who is this?' from Job's own 14:1 — a dying man unequal to the task.
Clarke: who pretendest to speak on the deep things of God and leavest them darker; Wesley fixes 'counsel' as God's providence in afflicting Job, the first word that struck him and is echoed at 42:3.

outliers.note: Reads the reproof as a mercy against pride: God must chasten the victorious Job lest the consciousness of virtue destroy the soul the scourges could not overcome.

themes: darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge

schools.summary: Gill hears a soldier's summons — gird the loins for battle, an eastern custom — daring Job to make good the arguments he had blustered.

Clarke: the Lord will not confound Job with terrors but bids him act kegeber, like a hero, and answer questions easier than those he had discussed; the interrogative method is the most convincing (Cicero against Catiline). Wesley adds the warrior's girding for battle.

themes: gird up thy loins like a man

schools.summary: Gill: the earth's firm foundations are nothing but the power and will of God (and the upholding Son); Job, a mere nonentity at creation, presumes to dive into Providence.
Henry sets the greatness of God ('I laid the foundations') against the meanness of man ('where wast thou?'): we were not in being; only Christ, the eternal Wisdom (Prov. 8:22; John 1:1), was present.
Clarke: thou art of yesterday, what canst thou know? Didst thou see me create the world? Wesley: dost thou presume to judge eternal counsels, when God settled the earth firm on its own centre?
Ellicott notes the creation-as-building metaphor is a concession to man's feebleness that heightens the force of the inevitable answer.

themes: where wast thou when I laid the foundations
the greatness of God and meanness of man

schools.summary: Gill: the Lord laid the measures, doing all by weight and measure; the mathematicians who claim the earth's circumference disagree, and 'if thou knowest' may be read 'for thou knowest' — a sarcasm.
Clarke reads an unfathomable depth of design (polar/equatorial distances, zones, magnitude, gravity, orbit); Wesley keeps the plain image of the measuring-line regulating every dimension.
Keil sets the verse in the primeval stages — tohu-vabohu then tehom — the question passing over the watery chaos to the ordered founding that follows.

themes: the line stretched upon the earth
the primeval chaos and the ordered work

schools.summary: Gill weighs the guesses (Ben Gersom's pillars, Aben Ezra's mountains) but grounds all on 'nothing but the mighty hand of God,' recalling that he hangs the earth on nothing (26:7).

Clarke asks how the earth revolves in space and what supports it, fastened as with a key-stone; Wesley: the building has no foundation but God's power, established upon itself, the corner-stone binding the walls so it cannot be moved.

themes: the earth upheld by God's hand alone
a house that cannot be moved

schools.summary: Gill ranges the senses: the stars literally, or the angels (as most), or good men and ministers (stars in Christ's hand), with Christ himself the principal morning star.

Clarke takes the morning stars and sons of God as one angelic host, made before the visible world (Gen. 1:1), the Chaldee's 'troops of angels' celebrating the work; Wesley agrees, noting the angels neither advised nor censured, as Job presumed to do.
Ellicott reads the angels entrusted with the stars' guardianship, whence Milton drew his conceptions; the sublimity needs no comment.

debates.question: Are the 'morning stars' the literal stars or the angels?

sides.position: literal stars (or ministers, or Christ the chief morning star), among other senses
the angelic host, one with the 'sons of God'

themes: the sons of God shouted for joy
creation greeted with praise, not fault-finding

schools.summary: Gill reads the sea's first creation, not the flood: the ocean an infant in embryo, shut in the bowels of the earth as in a womb, the chaos a woman big with child.

Clarke calls it a fine metaphor — the newborn sea issuing from the womb of chaos, the bursting waters alluded to; Wesley: who set bounds to the raging ocean and shut it with doors that it might not overflow the earth?

themes: who shut up the sea with doors
the sea as a new-born infant
the taming of the deep at its birth
the doors of the flood not hung by man

schools.summary: Gill keeps the figure: the cloud the garment for the new-born babe, the sea.
Keil renders clouds round the sea as a garment and thick mist as its swaddling-clothes, part of the ordered wrapping and bounding of the deep.

Clarke sees the receiving-cloth and first dressings of an infant (Mr. Good: the image 'exquisitely maintained'), with allusion to the darkness on the deep (Gen. 1:2); Wesley: God covered the sea with its own rising vapours as a garment, the dark clouds its swaddling-bands — though God alone truly bounds the sea.
Gill (with Broughton) has God cleaving the earth into a chasm to hold the waters, raising hills and sinking valleys as channels — a cradle for the swaddled sea, the second day's work.
Clarke refers 'bars and doors' to Gen. 1:9: the dry land the barrier, rivers and bays the doors; Wesley: God made the hollows as a cradle and fixed the sea's bounds as with bars and doors.
Ellicott prefers 'prescribed for it my decree,' marvelling that so vast and unstable a sea acknowledges any limits at all.

themes: brake up for it my decreed place
cradle and prison of the sea
bounds set to a restless thing

schools.summary: Gill hears the bare word of command: the waters wash their shores and run up the rivers and return, keeping to time and place, spoken by Jehovah the Word and obeyed by almighty power.

Clarke traces the restraint through the mechanics of the tides — lunar and solar attraction, the earth's rotation, and gravitation to the sea's own centre — the 'bars and doors' being these balanced laws that prevent too great a flux or ebb.

themes: hitherto shalt thou come, but no further
command and the mechanics of the tides
a bound the sea cannot pass

schools.summary: Gill: Job saw many a morning but could never command one, obliged to wait for a light he could not hasten.
Henry opens the 'six things': the morning is not ours to command or alter, the dayspring knew its place before we knew ours (Ps. 19:1); he hears in it the dayspring from on high of Luke 1:78.

Clarke reads the twilight of refracted rays and the shifting daybreak-points through the year's revolution; Wesley: didst thou create the sun and appoint day and night, teaching the dawn its varying time and place?
Ellicott: the dayspring is caused to know its place, changing from day to day with the seasons.

themes: the twilight and the shifting dawn

schools.summary: Gill: the light swiftly reaches the ends of the earth, applied to the gospel directed by Providence to the world's ends.
Keil: the dawn takes the carpet of the earth by the edges and shakes off the evil-doers who lay on it by night; Ellicott fixes the figure of a man shaking out a cloth (24:15-17).

Clarke pictures thieves and murderers fleeing the light like beasts, and reorders v.15 to follow v.13 (v.14 disturbing it); Wesley: the light shakes the wicked from the earth, discovering them, the morning being the time of judgment.

outliers.note: Judges verse 15 to belong immediately with verse 13, its connection disturbed by the intervening verse 14.

themes: take hold of the ends of the earth
the earth shaken like a garment
the dawn as minister of justice

schools.summary: Gill: as clay takes form under the seal, the earth (a mere tohu-bohu by night) is seen in beauty when the light comes — an emblem of the gospel's change in men.

Clarke: the earth like soft clay takes endless forms (Eastern clay-seals), decked like a stamped garment; he corrects Good's 'mould,' since light-rays never bend but travel straight. Wesley: the seal beautifies formless clay, so the light dresses the confused night-earth in order and glory.
Ellicott renders 'changed as clay under the seal, and all things stand forth as in their proper raiment,' the daylight giving shape to what darkness left formless.

outliers.note: Turns aside to the optics of the figure, insisting that rays of light never bend ('a gun might as well shoot round a corner') and correcting Mr. Good's rendering of clay to a mould.

themes: turned as clay to the seal

schools.summary: Gill: the wicked's 'light' is the darkness that was their day, withdrawn at dawn; figuratively the light of prosperity removed, or the light of life when they are sent into utter darkness.

Wesley weighs the two withholdings — by the wicked's own choice of darkness, or by the judgment of God or the magistrate cutting them off from the light of the living; the 'high arm' is their oppressing strength, now broken.

themes: from the wicked their light is withholden
the dawn as servant of moral order

schools.summary: Gill canvasses the renderings — subterranean springs, fountains at the bottom, 'drops,' the Targum's 'perplexities,' rocks and borders — each turned into the same unanswerable challenge.

Clarke: of these springs we know as much as Job, the depths unfathomed to this day; Wesley notes the Hebrew 'tears' of the sea, and argues that one who cannot sound the sea cannot fathom God's counsels.
Ellicott prefers the mazes and secret recesses of the trackless deep, leading on to the bottomless pit of death in v.17.

debates.question: What are the 'springs of the sea'?

sides.position: subterranean springs or fountains supplying the sea
the mazes and secret recesses of the trackless deep
the 'tears' of the sea, its outflowing fountains (Hebrew)

themes: the deep as emblem of God's counsels

schools.summary: Gill: not the gates by which death entered the world but those by which men pass into the state of the dead — never thrown open for mortals to look within.
Keil renders 'were the gates of death unveiled to thee... the gates of the realm of shades?', carrying the survey down into the underworld.

Clarke marks maveth and tsalmaveth (the intermediate state), death being as inexplicable as animal life, no mere privation; Wesley meditates on death as a grand secret, the world of spirits known only as blind men know colours.

themes: the doors of the shadow of death

schools.summary: Gill takes 'breadth' for all the earth's dimensions: not a Methuselah's lifetime could survey its every part, and some regions are simply inaccessible.
Clarke sets it in its ancient horizon: the globe's circumference then unknown, the earth supposed a vast plain bordered by ocean and sky.
Ellicott would render 'comprehended,' grants the plain-earth conception, yet insists the majestic sublimity of the language is not one whit affected by its unscientific frame.

themes: ignorance of the ground we walk

schools.summary: Gill reads an inquiry after the road to light's home and what that place may be — a home no traveller has found.

Clarke probes the physics (light was before the sun — what is light? is darkness mere privation?), owning philosophy still cannot say; Wesley strings the questions: where does light lodge, whither goes the sun, what way came light into a dark world — was Job privy to it?
Gill: to take the light by the hand and guide it to its bound is God's work alone, who steers the sun in its circuit so it never misses its way.

Clarke hears a biting irony — light and darkness personified with local dwellings — rendering it 'thou canst take Us to its boundary,' a taunt to humble Job's knowing pride; Wesley keeps the plain sense of leading the light over its whole course.
Ellicott glosses soberly: 'that thou shouldest take it' means to go with, or track, the light to its home.

outliers.note: Reads the verse as sustained sarcasm ('thou canst take Us to its boundary'), whose whole design is to humble Job's pride of knowledge.

themes: take the light to its bound
light and darkness with local dwellings
the irony of an impossible errand

schools.summary: Gill lets the impossibility answer itself: Job was not present at the dividing of light, and had he been the first man he came too late, man being made on the sixth day.
Clarke hears a biting irony, the plain translation confirming it: 'Thou knowest, because thou wast then born, and the number of thy days is great (rabbim).'
Ellicott would read the verse without interrogation as sublime irony: 'Doubtless thou knowest, for thou wast born then, and thy days are so great!'

debates.question: Is the verse a question or an ironic statement?

sides.position: an interrogation whose answer is shamed silence (as the AV)
a flat ironic statement, mock-praise of Job's antiquity

themes: knowest thou, because thou wast then born
a creature of the sixth day
the humbling of v.4 turned to sarcasm

schools.summary: Gill: the clouds are the storehouse of snow and hail, called 'treasures' as hidden, at God's command, and enriching — not literal heaps but produced instantly at his will.

Clarke on their formation (hail frozen spherules, both owing to electricity), noting hail alone yields no apparent good, while frost is 'God's universal plough'; Wesley keeps the wonder of the storehouse God draws from when he sees fit.

themes: the treasures of the snow and hail
not literal heaps but instant production

schools.summary: Gill: the snow and hail reserved for the punishment and affliction of men, kept ready for the appointed hour.

Keil carries the passage forward (the reserved stores, the parted light, the watercourse and lightning-path) and marks that rain, dew, ice, and frost have no created father or mother; Ellicott points to the stones cast on the fleeing kings and the hail of Ps. 18:13.

Clarke renders 'the season of strictness' (bound by frost) and refers the 'day of battle' to hail as God's weapon — the plague on Egypt (Exod. 9:23) and the shower on the Canaanite kings (Josh. 10:11).

themes: reserved against the day of battle
the arsenal of snow and hail
the folly of striving with God

schools.summary: Gill lists the ways daylight is 'parted' — creation, sunrise/set, the hemispheres and poles, the climates, Egypt dark and Goshen light — setting aside the lightning reading since lightning comes later.

Clarke reads the lightning and thunder-cloud, its zigzag 'parting' unaccountable, the east wind the euroclydon; Wesley takes the daylight variously distributed, the sun the 'father of the winds' raising the east wind.
Ellicott keeps the daylight distributed in turn to all the earth, the east wind naturally rising with the dawn.

debates.question: Does the 'light' here mean the daylight or the lightning?

sides.position: the daylight, parted and distributed over the earth
the lightning, whose zigzag path is the 'parting'

themes: by what way is the light parted
the scattering of the east wind
the untraceable path of the light

schools.summary: Henry marks the turn from Job's ignorance to his impotence: God has sovereign dominion over the waters and the lightning, directing every drop and preparing the lightnings for the rain (Ps. 135:7).
Gill reads the 'watercourse' as a channel in the atmosphere, God steering the rain to fall gently in measured drops where he pleases (Jarchi: every drop its own canal).

Clarke suspects a cloud or waterspout (the root 'to ascend' = evaporation) and renders 'a path for the bolt of thunder,' God the true Thunderer; Wesley: the showers led orderly as through pipes, the lightning let out of its cloud-prison.
Ellicott renders the opening 'cleft a channel for the water-flood.'

themes: a watercourse for the overflowing waters
a way for the lightning of thunder
God the Thunderer directs every drop

schools.summary: Gill: the rain falls on barren, uninhabited land for the sake of the wild beasts, showing God's care even for them — an emblem of the gospel-rain on the Gentile wilderness.
Clarke: the cloud is led over deserts with no human inhabitant to make the tender herb spring for the beasts, fowls, and insects God sustains; Wesley: rain poured where no man waters it by art.

themes: bounty that looks for no return

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the doubled 'desolate and waste' ground, thirsty as one that never says 'enough,' yet satisfied by God — a figure of grace satisfying dry souls.
Clarke: the desert made to bud for the sake of its beasts and insects, all sustained by God; Wesley marks the turn from convincing Job of ignorance to convincing him of impotence.

themes: the bud of the tender herb

schools.summary: Gill: the rain has no father but God alone, whatever the secondary causes — a figure of the gospel, likewise not of men but a gift come down from heaven.

Clarke stays baffled by the dew (the egley, small globules), the philosophers undecided whether it rises from the earth or descends from the air; Wesley: can any man beget or produce rain at his pleasure?

themes: no created father, no human maker
God as the dew unto Israel

schools.summary: Gill: the ice is God's child, and where v.28 spoke of a father this speaks of a womb, God represented as a mother (Orpheus' metropator, mother-father at once).
Keil balances the figure: rain and dew have no created father, ice and hoar-frost no created mother, the parallel asking after both the begetter and the bearer.
Clarke on the nature of ice (lighter than water, floating by its air-bubbles) and hoar-frost (congealed dew in crystals), owning that after 2000-3000 years we know about as much as Job.

themes: out of whose womb came the ice
God as mother of the winter

schools.summary: Gill: the frost makes the water's surface hard as stone to bear carriages where ships went, an emblem of the hard heart thawed only by the Spirit and the Sun of righteousness.
Clarke sets it in winter (the coming constellations rise then): the deep frozen not only at the poles but through the northern countries, locked from navigation for months.
Ellicott renders 'the waters hide themselves and become like stone,' water losing its quality and turned to stone.

themes: the waters hid as with a stone
the face of the deep frozen
the frozen heart and the thaw of grace

schools.summary: Gill: the Pleiades' spring-influence cannot be restrained (a figure of efficacious grace); some read 'bands of the Pleiades' — either way Job can neither bind their influence nor break their band.

Clarke sets Pleiades (spring) against Orion (winter) but is reluctant to follow the confident constellation-names, citing Coverdale; Wesley: God can change the seasons, binding the Pleiades and loosing Orion, but we cannot.
Ellicott weighs 'sweet influences' as either astral influence or a chain/band binding the cluster, judging the parallel 'bands of Orion' to favour the second.

debates.question: Do the 'sweet influences of Pleiades' mean astral influences or the cords binding the cluster?

sides.position: the influences the constellation pours out upon the seasons
the chain or band that ties the seven stars together

outliers.note: Confesses a reluctance to follow the learned on the constellation-names, not seeing the groundwork, and cites Coverdale's older rendering.

schools.summary: Gill leans to Mazzaroth as 'the chambers of the south,' the hidden southern stars (from a root 'to separate'), or else the twelve signs of the Zodiac brought forth by the Lord.
Keil renders the signs of the Zodiac and the guiding of the Bear with its children; Ellicott takes Mazzaroth as the Zodiac and 'the children of Arcturus' as the three stars in the Bear's tail.
Wesley reads Mazzaroth as the southern signs and Arcturus as the northern with its attendant lesser stars; Clarke reports Parkhurst's guess that Mazzaroth is the simoom, the pestilential summer wind.

sides.position: the southern constellations, the 'chambers of the south'
the twelve signs of the Zodiac
the simoom, a pestilential summer wind (Parkhurst, as reported by Clarke)

themes: stars named and guided by God alone

schools.summary: Gill: the 'ordinances of heaven' are God's decreed, stable laws of the stars' situation, motion, and influence, not made by men nor even fully known.
Clarke asks the astronomer whether he knows the planetary laws, noting Newton could not say what gravity is; Wesley: did Job give these laws, or can he over-rule their influence on the world?
Ellicott glosses the ordinances as the recurring seasons and their power of influencing the earth.

themes: the dominion of heaven on earth
laws unmade and uncomprehended by man
the sky's order rebukes the arraigning of Providence

schools.summary: Gill: Job cannot magisterially command the clouds for rain; it is had only in a suppliant way, by the prayer of faith as Elijah's (cf. Zech. 10:1), not by dictate.
Clarke sets Job's voice (kolecha) against the voice of Jehovah: thunder is koloth, 'voices,' the voice of God — the feeble man cannot summon what the Almighty commands.

themes: lift up thy voice to the clouds
the prayer of faith, not command
man's voice against the voice of God

schools.summary: Gill pictures the lightning as a servant reporting 'Here we are'; only God commands it — Elijah's fire not to be imitated (the disciples reproved, Luke 9:54), lest men wield such power.
Keil: what is denied to man's natural power is possible to faith, as Elijah shows.

Clarke contrasts the pagan Jupiter the Thunderer with the true Almighty ('who can thunder with a voice like his?'), noting berakim carries sense and sound — will the lightnings be Job's messengers as they are God's?

themes: the flash that reports 'Here we are'
the lightning obeys its Maker alone

schools.summary: Gill takes the wisdom of the inward parts for the mind of man, no such star-guiding wisdom being lodged in him.

Clarke reads the understanding of the contemplative man, helpless without the Almighty's inspiration, but reports Good's 'vollies,' the Septuagint's 'weaving,' and the Vulgate's 'cock' proclaiming the night-watches.
Ellicott owns the perplexity and offers, with Good, to refer 'the inward parts' to the lightnings personified: 'who hath put such understanding in their inward parts?'

debates.question: What are the 'inward parts' given wisdom?

sides.position: the mind or heart of man
the lightnings personified, given discernment to run their errands

outliers.note: Reports the ancient versions' divergent renderings: the Septuagint's 'knowledge of weaving' and the Vulgate's 'understanding to the cock' that proclaims the night-watches.

themes: reason itself a gift of God

schools.summary: Gill: none can number or 'declare' the clouds; he records Aben Ezra's and Broughton's 'who can make them as sapphire?' — make a clear sky when it is overcast.
Clarke suggests 'number' may mean to irradiate (the sky's inimitable tinges), and explains the 'bottles of heaven' as the clouds, after the skin water-bottles (girbahs).
Ellicott weighs 'stay the bottles' in two opposite senses — pouring out or laying up in store — the context uncertain; with this verse the survey of physical phenomena ends.

debates.question: Does 'stay the bottles of heaven' mean to pour them out or to hold them back?

sides.position: to pour out the bottles in rain
to lay them up in store, holding the rain back

themes: to pour out or to hold back
the clouds keep their count and contents from man

schools.summary: Gill: the dust ground into powder and the clods cleaving as if glued, whether in drought or when the bottles of heaven are poured out — the rain brought down to the soil.
Clarke asks the mystery of cohesion — how dust was concreted and clods cohere — instancing the ruby, opal, lapis lazuli, and emerald, worthless dusts grown into hardness in a way known only to God.

themes: from the highest cloud to the hardening dust

schools.summary: Gill marks the turn to animals, beginning boldly with the lion: not man but God hunts its prey (the reputed jackal going before it, the young lions feeding the old).

Clarke turns it on Job's faculties (he has neither the lion's strength, instinct, nor cunning) and notes ch. 39 should begin here as natural history opens; Wesley: is it by Job's care that the desert lions are fed?
Ellicott agrees the new chapter ought to begin here, the animal creation now passing under review.

themes: wilt thou hunt the prey for the lion
the appetite of the young lions
providence over the beasts of prey

schools.summary: Gill weighs whether these are old lions couching for want of strength, and reads the lurking beasts as emblems of cruel tyrants lying in wait with murder and rapine.
Keil notes the Hebrew wealth of lion-names (cf. 4:10) and that the lioness, named first, provides for her whelps that couch with her.
Clarke: the young lions lie in covert to surprise prey they cannot outrun, whence kephirim takes its name from a root 'to cover or hide' (cf. 4:11).

themes: the covert to lie in wait
the Hebrew names for the lion

schools.summary: Gill: not man but God feeds the ravens, creatures voracious, mean, and useless, yet not overlooked.

Clarke notes the raven chosen for its hungry, importunate cry (a hated bird of ill omen), citing Young's paraphrase of the crying brood; Wesley marks the descent from the lion to the contemptible raven, whose forsaken young God feeds — will he not much more provide for his children?
Ellicott fixes the grammar: 'they wander for lack of meat' is dependent — 'when his young ones cry unto God, when they wander for lack of meat.'

outliers.note: Enriches the verse with Dr. Young's poetic paraphrase of the raven's crying brood, and the old fancy that the raven's importunate voice is always calling upon Providence.

themes: the young ones cry unto God
the God of greatness the God of care
